items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The British government has approved drilling at a controversial North Sea gas field, despite strong opposition from environmental groups. Energy companies welcomed the decision and predicted the project could supply over six percent of the nation’s gas at peak production. Officials argue that developing domestic resources is necessary to boost national energy security while global conflicts drive up fuel costs. The prime minister stated that although the country remains committed to long-term climate targets, oil and gas will still be needed during the transition to renewable energy. However, climate activists and politicians heavily criticized the approval and warned that increased fossil fuel reliance won’t lower household energy bills because prices are dictated by international markets. They stress that true security requires a faster shift toward clean energy rather than expanding fossil fuel infrastructure. Difficult words: controversial (causing a lot of angry public discussion and strong disagreement), dictate (to state, order, or control authoritatively how something must be done or decide), reliance (dependence on someone or something for help or support). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The UK government approved a new project to drill for gas in the North Sea. Energy companies say this project will help produce more gas for the country. Leaders argue that using local gas makes the country safer as global conflict causes energy prices to rise. The prime minister explained that the country still needs gas while moving toward green energy. Environmental groups and green politicians strongly disagree with the plan. They warn that drilling produces harmful emissions and will not lower electricity bills for normal families. Activists argue that the government should focus on renewable energy like wind and solar instead of fossil fuels. Difficult words: approve (to officially agree), harmful (when something hurts living things or the planet), renewable energy (energy from natural sources, such as wind, sun, and so on). items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The UK government says yes to getting new gas from under the sea. There is a plan to drill in the North Sea. Leaders say that this gas will help keep the country safe when energy prices are high. The prime minister says that the country still needs gas, but it also wants clean energy in the future. Many people are very angry about this decision . They say that getting more gas is bad for the planet. It will not help people get cheaper electricity. They want the government to use clean power like wind and sun instead of oil and gas. Difficult words: drill (to make a hole in the earth to get oil or gas), price (how much money something costs), decision (what you do after thinking or talking about it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Salmon farming and tech
items.text: Salmon farming is a growing, multi-billion-dollar industry. The biggest producers, Norway and Chile, have seen booming profits; however, the industry is facing problems such as mass salmon die-offs, infectious diseases, and environmental damage. Fish farming relies heavily on chemicals and antibiotics to treat parasites that can weaken or kill the fish. A large farm in Norway, Norlock, uses freshwater baths and chemical treatments to combat salmon lice, but these methods can also stress the fish and lead to further health issues. One innovative solution at Norlock involves using laser technology to remove the parasites, reducing infection rates. Also, farms in open sea environments benefit from ocean currents, which can help wash away waste and reduce diseases. Chile’s salmon farms, which are heavily dependent on antibiotics, are also under scrutiny for their environmental impact. New methods like closed aquaculture systems, which keep farmed fish in tanks and prevent contamination, offer hope for a more sustainable future in salmon farming. Difficult words: parasite (an organism that lives in or on an organism and feeds from it), innovative (featuring new methods), scrutiny (critical and detailed examination). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Salmon farming and tech
items.text: Salmon farming is a big business and Norway and Chile are the leading producers of farmed salmon. The industry makes billions of dollars, but issues like diseases, fish deaths, and parasites are becoming hard to control. In Norway, farms like Norlock are trying to reduce the number of sick fish. They use chemicals, freshwater baths, and even lasers to kill parasites. But even with these new technologies, salmon farming has a lot of problems. Farmed salmon often escape from the nets and can spread disease to wild salmon. In Chile, salmon farms use large amounts of antibiotics to fight diseases, but this can also harm the environment and human health. Some salmon farms are trying new methods, like closed aquaculture, where they keep fish in tanks instead of in open water. This could help make salmon farming more sustainable in the future. Difficult words: parasite (an animal or plant which lives on another animal or plant and feeds from it), escape (to get free from a place), antibiotic (a medicine which destroys bacteria in the body). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Salmon farming and tech
items.text: Salmon farming is a big business. But it has some problems. Norway and Chile are the biggest salmon producers. The fish often get sick or die. Small parasites attack the fish and make them weak . It is not easy to stop the parasites. Some farms, like Norlock in Norway, use chemicals, fresh water, and even lasers to kill them. In Chile, farms use a lot of medicine to keep the fish healthy. But this can hurt the environment . Some farms are now trying a new way of farming. They use big tanks instead of open water. This could help make salmon farming better for the environment. Difficult words: parasite (an animal or plant which lives on another and feeds from it), weak (not strong enough), environment (the natural world). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Man sells everything for AI dream "partner"
items.text: A man in Brazil had a sad experience in his search for love. Mr X, 49, sold everything he owned to get enough money to see a woman he met online. He travelled over 2,000 kilometres by bus. He first met her online in 2020 and fell in love with her. He wanted to marry her. Her name was Jessica. Her online profile read: "I really want to support you. I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life." Mr X went to meet her in the city of Belo Horizonte, but he could not find her. He showed people photos of her, but nobody knew who she was. He then found out that she was not real. She was created by AI. The man was sad. He said: "I came here to find happiness." Mr X's story shows how risky it can be to look for love online. Many people feel lonely and want to find a partner. However, they can be easily tricked because AI can make people who look and sound real. Jessica's social media account had over 300,000 followers. She looked like a real woman. The person who created Jessica said they made her to get people's attention online. They wanted to use the AI Jessica to help sell things. Mr X wants people to be careful so they don't make a similar mistake in the future. It is important to check the identity of a person you meet online carefully. items.title: One billion meals thrown away every day
items.text: More than one billion meals are thrown away worldwide every day, despite famine and millions of people starving. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) recently reported that households are responsible for 60 per cent of food waste, followed by restaurants and food services at 28 per cent, and shops at 12 per cent. The Maldives has the highest estimated household food waste per person, at around 260 kilograms annually. Syria, Seychelles, Mexico and Tunisia also recorded high levels. Globally, food waste accounts for 8 to 10 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions. As discarded food decomposes in landfills, it releases the dangerous greenhouse gas methane, which accelerates global warming. Individuals, businesses and governments can all take practical steps to reduce food waste. People should plan meals, prepare shopping lists, and purchase only what they need. We should store ingredients correctly and freeze surplus portions. We should also turn leftovers into new dishes and compost inedible waste. Restaurants and supermarkets also have a huge part to play in reducing food loss. They can donate surplus food to communities in need. Martin Krause, Director of the Climate Change Division at UNEP, said: "Every meal rescued, shared or never wasted is food put to better use."
